import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Combinatorial representation of the recurrence $a(n+2) = 2a(n+1) + 2a(n)$

A028859 (OEIS): $a(n+2) = 2 \cdot a(n+1) + 2 \cdot a(n)$; $a(0) = 1$, $a(1) = 3$.

*References:*
- [A028859](https://oeis.org/A028859)
- [arxiv/2605.22763](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.22763) *Advancing Mathematics Research with AI-Driven Formal Proof Search* by George Tsoukalas et al.
-/

namespace OeisA28859


/--
A028859 (OEIS): $a(n+2) = 2 \cdot a(n+1) + 2 \cdot a(n)$; $a(0) = 1$, $a(1) = 3$.
-/
def a (n : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  match n with
  | 0 => 1
  | 1 => 3
  | (n + 2) => 2 * a (n + 1) + 2 * a n
termination_by n

set_option linter.unusedVariables false


@[category test, AMS 11]
lemma a_0 : a 0 = 1 := by native_decide

@[category test, AMS 11]
lemma a_1 : a 1 = 3 := by native_decide

@[category test, AMS 11]
lemma a_2 : a 2 = 8 := by native_decide

@[category test, AMS 11]
lemma a_3 : a 3 = 22 := by native_decide

@[category test, AMS 11]
lemma a_4 : a 4 = 60 := by native_decide


/--
Conjecture: The sequence a(n) is also the number of compositions of $n$ into positive integers
such that adjacent parts and the largest part differ by at most 1. - _Gus Wiseman_, May 19 2020

A formal proof has been found with the methods described in
[arxiv/2605.22763](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.22763).
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using formal_conjectures at
"https://github.com/mo271/formal-conjectures/blob/a32396489dcb8f86c3549b93aa358ac6a10a3a1f/FormalConjectures/OEIS/28859.wip.lean#L402"]
theorem exists_finset_sequence (n : ℕ) :
    let L := n + 1
    let Sequence := Fin L → ℕ
    let S : Set Sequence :=
      {σ : Sequence |
        L > 0 ∧
          (∀ i : Fin L, σ i > 0) ∧
            let max_val := Finset.sup Finset.univ σ
            (∀ k : ℕ, 1 ≤ k ∧ k ≤ max_val → ∃ i : Fin L, σ i = k) ∧
            (∀ i j : Fin L, i < j → j.val ≠ i.val + 1 → σ i ≥ σ j)}
    ∃ (F : Finset Sequence), (F : Set Sequence) = S ∧ F.card = a n := by
    sorry

end OeisA28859

findings.description: The docstring at lines 62–63 describes compositions summing to n, with adjacent/largest-part differences at most 1. Neither the cited conjecture nor the Lean statement says this. Both concern length-(n+1) sequences whose values form an initial interval of positive integers and whose nonadjacent entries are weakly decreasing. For example, Lean admits (3,1,2) when n=2, although its sum is 6 and its first adjacent difference is 2. The declaration's mathematical statement is faithful; only its description is wrong.
findings.source_evidence: OEIS A028859, Gus Wiseman's May 19, 2020 comment: “Also the number of length n + 1 sequences that cover an initial interval of positive integers and whose non-adjacent parts are weakly decreasing.” https://oeis.org/A028859. Xinjun Wang's linked paper, Theorem 1, explicitly states the same length-indexed interpretation: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20437247.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace the docstring's first paragraph with: “The sequence a(n) counts sequences of length n+1 whose set of values is an initial interval of positive integers and whose non-adjacent entries are weakly decreasing. — Gus Wiseman, May 19, 2020.” Leave the Lean statement unchanged.

reformulations.difference: The source counts normal sequences directly. Lean encodes normality using positivity and coverage up to Finset.sup, and expresses the count as existence of a Finset whose coercion equals the entire admissible set.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Put L=n+1 and M=Finset.univ.sup σ. Positivity and the coverage condition are equivalent to the range being {1,…,M}, with M≥1 because L is nonzero. The index conditions i<j and j.val≠i.val+1 are exactly separation by at least two positions. Coverage forces M≤L, so all entries are bounded by L and the admissible set is finite. Consequently, existence of F with ↑F=S and F.card=c is equivalent to S having cardinality c. These equivalences were proved for arbitrary c, and the complete original statement was proved equivalent to the source formulation in /workspace/review/scratch.lean, without using the imported sorry theorem.

https://arxiv.org/e-print/2605.22763 (v2 TeX source, OEIS discussion and proof-source references)
